14	# Rules - Conciseness
15	
16	The conciseness layer above the Human Voice card: what to cut, what is never cut, and the test that decides which is which.
17	
18	**Loading Condition:** ALWAYS, and rules only. A file paid for on every turn stays small enough to be worth paying for
19	**Purpose:** Carries the cut rules, the keep rules and the reconstruction test that decides between them, so every delivery is sized as well as checked for banned wording
20	**Scope:** Quantity, structure and load-bearing-ness, so an artifact that clears every hard blocker is not still three times too long. Nothing routes to it, since being ALWAYS-loaded is what makes it unroutable
21	**Output Path:** None. The layer governs the length of an artifact another file writes, and produces none of its own
22	**Loads With:** the consuming system's skill entry and `Rules - Human Voice Core`. That card governs word choice and this file governs quantity, so both run on every delivery
23	**Authority:** `Rules - Conciseness - On Demand Rationale` carries the reason behind every rule below, the vocabulary candidates that were refused, the worked cut and keep pairs, and the roster of what blocks against what advises. Load it ON_DEMAND before changing a rule, never in order to write one. Both files share one numbering, so a section present in one and absent here lives there and keeps its number. That is why this card runs 5, 7, 8, 12 rather than counting straight, and why renumbering it would break the Section 8 citations three skills carry
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. THE TWO-SIDED CONTRACT
28	
29	Cuts and keeps here are edits rather than scored penalties, so they never count toward a system's hard blocker total. The two halves are load-bearing in equal measure: read only the cut half and the output arrives compressed until the reasoning falls out of it, and read only the keep half and nothing ever gets shorter. Every rule the validator blocks on arrives in a pair at the same strength, so the gate cannot be satisfied by cutting alone.
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 2. THE RECONSTRUCTION TEST
34	
35	After a cut, could a reader who does not already know the answer recover what was removed from what remains? If yes, the cut was free. If no, the information moved into the reader's head, which is loss wearing the shape of compression. Apply it per cut and never per document, because a document-level verdict is a judgement about length and length is the judgement that strips connectives. The reader it asks about is the one who opens the artifact three weeks later with no memory of the conversation that produced it.
36	
37	---
38	
39	## 3. CUT RULES
40	
41	### 3.1 The named rules
42	
43	- **Question echo.** An opening that restates the prompt before answering it
44	- **Intent narration.** Announcing the move instead of making it
45	- **Compliance acknowledgement.** Agreeing to do the work at the top of the work
46	- **Terminal recap.** A closing paragraph that repeats the body, even accurately
47	- **Hedge stack.** Two or more uncertainty markers on one claim. Keep the one that is true
48	- **Importance assertion.** A sentence whose only content is that something matters
49	- **The conclusion move.** The whole paragraph, not only the phrase that opens it
50	- **Both-sides padding.** Symmetric pro and con on a question that is not symmetric
51	- **Empty enumeration.** Naming that there are several things, listing them, analysing none
52	- **Heading echo.** A first sentence that restates its own heading
53	- **Restated constraint.** Repeating back a fact the user supplied
54	- **Effort reporting.** Narrating the work done rather than what it found
55	- **Count padding.** An item added so a list carries a different number of items. The triad rule counts triads per 150 words and bans none, so leave the count alone and cut something that was never load-bearing
56	
57	### 3.2 The stated vocabulary
58	
59	The validator blocks on exactly the terms below, so this list and the gate are one list, and adding a term to either alone is the drift that kept these checks advisory. Section 3.3 of the on-demand rationale records every candidate refused, with the correct writing each would have failed.
60	
61	Never open a sentence with: "In conclusion", "In summary", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "It's worth noting", "It is worth noting", "It's important to note", "It is important to note", "Let's explore", "Let's dive in", "Let's take a look", "At the end of the day", "Without further ado", "As we all know", "It goes without saying", "First and foremost", "Last but not least", "With that in mind", "On that note", "That said", "Needless to say", "Simply put", "In essence", "At its core", "In the world of", "When it comes to", "At a high level", "As you can see", "As mentioned above", "As noted above", "As previously noted", "As we have seen", "As discussed above", "In this section", "Put simply", "Generally speaking", "Broadly speaking", "The key takeaway", "The fact of the matter is", "It should be noted", "It must be noted", "By way of background".
62	
63	Never close a section on: "In summary", "In conclusion", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "In short", "All in all", "Overall", "Ultimately", "In closing", "To conclude", "To wrap up", "The takeaway", "Net net", "In a nutshell", "Long story short", "To put it simply", "On the whole".
64	
65	At most one hedge per claim: "might", "may", "could", "perhaps", "maybe", "possibly", "potentially", "probably", "seems", "appears", "arguably", "somewhat", "relatively", "presumably", "likely", "generally", "typically", "I think", "I believe", "tends to", "to some extent", "in some cases", "apparently", "conceivably", "ostensibly", "seemingly", "in theory", "I suspect", "My sense is".
66	
67	A cross-reference that names its target stays legitimate, so "As noted above" is banned while "the payout window defined under The weekly cycle" is not. A heading followed by a sentence that shares its words and adds no new one is a heading echo: cut the sentence and open on substance.
68	
69	### 3.4 The two cut rules the validator settles alone
70	
71	Both resolve without judgement, so the validator blocks on them in a deliverable and reports them as advice on an instruction file.
72	
73	**Importance assertion.** A sentence of twelve words or fewer carrying one of "important", "critical", "essential", "crucial", "vital", "matters", "significant", "noteworthy" or "fundamental", and carrying no content word of its own beyond that marker and generic filler. A sentence that names what matters and why is left alone.
74	
75	**Effort reporting.** A sentence opening on "I" or "We" that reaches one of "analysed", "analyzed", "reviewed", "checked", "scored", "scanned", "verified", "examined", "evaluated", "assessed", "investigated" or "audited" within the next few words. A quoted mention is left alone, and so is a sentence whose subject is the process the artifact documents rather than the author. State what the work found, since the work itself is not the deliverable.
76	
77	---
78	
79	## 4. KEEP RULES
80	
81	The anti-robotic half, at the same weight as the cut list. Each item names what a compression pass destroys first.
82	
83	- **Semantic connectives.** `because`, `so`, `which means`, `unless`, `otherwise`, `since` carry the logic, and deleting one turns an argument into a pile of assertions. The Human Voice cap on `however`, `furthermore`, `moreover`, `additionally` and `consequently` limits rhetoric and never reaches these
84	- **One concrete instance per non-obvious rule.** The example is what makes a rule applicable
85	- **The caveat that prevents a wrong action.** A reader who follows the trimmed version and breaks something was not served by the trim
86	- **The scope qualifier.** `when`, `only when`, `for X but not Y`. A rule stripped of its scope is applied everywhere
87	- **The noun behind a pronoun.** Name it again once the referent sits more than a clause away
88	- **The negative case.** "A path string is not verification" is where the reader learns the boundary
89	- **The specific number.** 33 fixtures, not several fixtures
90	- **One human beat per roughly 400 words.** An aside, a judgement, a plain admission of what is unknown
91	- **Grammar.** Articles, copulas and finite verbs are never a compression target, because conciseness removes claims and never syntax
92	
93	---
94	
95	## 5. OVER-COMPRESSION SIGNATURES
96	
97	### 5.1 The five shapes
98	
99	- **Connective stripping.** Clauses sit next to each other with the relation deleted, so the reader guesses whether the second causes, qualifies or contradicts the first
100	- **Referent stripping.** Pronouns and bare nouns left with their antecedents cut away
101	- **Telegraphese.** Dropped articles and copulas, verbless fragments, headline grammar in body text
102	- **Condition collapse.** A conditional rule flattened into an absolute one, which is a correctness bug rather than a style one
103	- **Example deletion.** An abstract rule left with nothing showing what it looks like in use
104	
105	### 5.2 The two the validator counts, and the perimeter they are measured over
106	
107	Connective stripping and telegraphese leave a numeric trace, so the validator counts them and blocks on a deliverable below either floor. Repair a document that trips one by naming the deleted relations back in and restoring the subject behind every stranded pronoun, never by adding words.
108	
109	- **Connective floor.** At least 5 semantic connectives per 1000 words of prose
110	- **Article floor.** At least 30 articles per 1000 words of prose
111	
112	Both floors are measured over paragraph prose alone, because a ratio only means something where sentences carry the reasoning. Outside the perimeter: frontmatter, a heading at any level, a bullet, a numbered item, a table row, a blockquote, an image, a horizontal rule, a field line such as `**Placement:** Creator deals dashboard`, a hashtag or handle run, a label line whose whole content is one bold or underlined run such as `**Most authentic**`, anything inside a fenced code block, and any HTML comment. Below 200 words of paragraph prose neither floor is applied, since a ratio over fewer words than that is noise.
113	
114	---
115	
116	## 7. FORMAT
117	
118	Prose, bullets and tables are not interchangeable, and picking wrong is how a short answer still reads badly. Three questions decide and the first yes wins: prose where the items differ in weight or their order encodes reasoning, a table where every row shares the same fields, bullets where the items are parallel, independently actionable and three to seven in number. Anything reaching the end without a yes is one paragraph pretending to be a list. Over-bulleting is the main way output turns robotic while looking concise, and the tells are verbless fragments, a bullet that needs the one above it to parse, and a list whose connectives were deleted so the items would line up. Heading density scales with length: under 300 words no headings, above that one per 150 to 400 words.
119	
120	---
121	
122	## 8. WHAT A DELIVERABLE NEVER CONTAINS
123	
124	The reasoning that produced an artifact, the score it earned and the assumptions it rests on are real work, and they belong in the reply beside the export path rather than inside the file the reader opens.
125	
126	### 8.1 The enumeration
127	
128	- A scoring section of any kind, whether headed MEQT, HVR, DEAL scoring, Scoring, Self-scan, Hard blockers or Weakest
129	- A dimension breakdown line, such as `M 4 · E 6 · Q 6 · T 3 · D 3` or its `D · E · A · L` equivalent
130	- A total, a floor status, a pass or fail verdict, or a score band action
131	- A hard blocker count or a voice self-scan line, in any wording
132	- Score commentary, such as a line opening `Weakest:` and naming which dimensions were thin
133	- An improvement-cycle note, an iteration count or a re-score history
134	- A bracketed `[Assumes: ...]` tag
135	- A methodology transcript, a perspective roster, an energy level or a phase-flow trace
136	- A validation checklist, a gate roster or a template-compliance report
137	- An attestation footer, a Mode header in visible text, a Template version in visible text, or any other processing metadata
138	
139	### 8.2 The one sanctioned exception
140	
141	Line 1 may carry a single HTML comment header, which renders as nothing and is the designed home for the mode, the framework, the score and the template version. A `Stats:` or `Assumes:` line written as an HTML comment directly below sits inside the same exception, for the same reason. Invisible when rendered is the whole test, so a score written as visible text is a violation wherever it sits in the file and a score written as a comment is fine wherever it sits.
142	
143	### 8.3 Where the reporting goes instead
144	
145	The reply carries what the artifact does not: the export path with read-back confirmation where the runtime can write files, the score and its verdict at the depth the mode calls for, the voice self-scan line naming the terms fixed and the terms kept with their reason, the assumptions in a form the user can correct before they harden, a short summary and one next step. Producing that report is the point, and moving it out of the artifact does not make it optional.
146	
147	### 8.4 Two narrow overrides
148	
149	Where the artifact refines a supplied source, never inject a Mode, Template, Perspectives, Quality Score or Energy header into preserved source structure, since the comment header is for a new artifact and a refinement keeps the source's own opening. Where the packaging renders the deliverable in a panel instead of saving a file, that rendered block is the artifact and the enumeration applies to it unchanged, the report follows the block, and the path is reported as export-equivalent rather than claimed as a save.
150	
151	---
152	
153	## 12. THE PRE-EXPORT PASS
154	
155	Run this after the voice pass and before the export, in order. The first two steps are the cut side and the last three are the keep side, and running only the cut side is the failure this layer exists to prevent.
156	
157	1. Delete every opener, recap and hedge stack named in Section 3.2, both shapes named in Section 3.4, and the question echo, intent narration, compliance acknowledgement and closing recap the body already carries, including the sentences after the phrase that opened one
158	2. Apply the reconstruction test to every remaining cut you are tempted to make, and stop at the first one that fails
159	3. Name every relation a reader would otherwise guess, then repair referent stripping, telegraphese and condition collapse in place
160	4. Confirm one concrete instance survives per non-obvious rule, one caveat survives per action that could go wrong, and the format matches the content under Section 7
161	5. Confirm the body carries nothing from Section 8.1, and that everything removed at this step now sits in the reply. This step is skipped most often, because the process material was correct work and deleting correct work feels wrong. It is not deleted, it moves
162

**Authority:** `Rules - Conciseness - On Demand Rationale` carries the reason behind every rule below, the vocabulary candidates that were refused, the worked cut and keep pairs, and the roster of what blocks against what advises. Load it ON_DEMAND before changing a rule, never in order to write one. Both files share one numbering, so a section present in one and absent here lives there and keeps its number. That is why this card runs 5, 7, 8, 12 rather than counting straight, and why renumbering it would break the Section 8 citations three skills carry

---

## 1. THE TWO-SIDED CONTRACT

Cuts and keeps here are edits rather than scored penalties, so they never count toward a system's hard blocker total. The two halves are load-bearing in equal measure: read only the cut half and the output arrives compressed until the reasoning falls out of it, and read only the keep half and nothing ever gets shorter. Every rule the validator blocks on arrives in a pair at the same strength, so the gate cannot be satisfied by cutting alone.

---

## 2. THE RECONSTRUCTION TEST

After a cut, could a reader who does not already know the answer recover what was removed from what remains? If yes, the cut was free. If no, the information moved into the reader's head, which is loss wearing the shape of compression. Apply it per cut and never per document, because a document-level verdict is a judgement about length and length is the judgement that strips connectives. The reader it asks about is the one who opens the artifact three weeks later with no memory of the conversation that produced it.

---

## 3. CUT RULES

### 3.1 The named rules

- **Question echo.** An opening that restates the prompt before answering it
- **Intent narration.** Announcing the move instead of making it
- **Compliance acknowledgement.** Agreeing to do the work at the top of the work
- **Terminal recap.** A closing paragraph that repeats the body, even accurately
- **Hedge stack.** Two or more uncertainty markers on one claim. Keep the one that is true
- **Importance assertion.** A sentence whose only content is that something matters
- **The conclusion move.** The whole paragraph, not only the phrase that opens it
- **Both-sides padding.** Symmetric pro and con on a question that is not symmetric
- **Empty enumeration.** Naming that there are several things, listing them, analysing none
- **Heading echo.** A first sentence that restates its own heading
- **Restated constraint.** Repeating back a fact the user supplied
- **Effort reporting.** Narrating the work done rather than what it found
- **Count padding.** An item added so a list carries a different number of items. The triad rule counts triads per 150 words and bans none, so leave the count alone and cut something that was never load-bearing

### 3.2 The stated vocabulary

The validator blocks on exactly the terms below, so this list and the gate are one list, and adding a term to either alone is the drift that kept these checks advisory. Section 3.3 of the on-demand rationale records every candidate refused, with the correct writing each would have failed.

Never open a sentence with: "In conclusion", "In summary", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "It's worth noting", "It is worth noting", "It's important to note", "It is important to note", "Let's explore", "Let's dive in", "Let's take a look", "At the end of the day", "Without further ado", "As we all know", "It goes without saying", "First and foremost", "Last but not least", "With that in mind", "On that note", "That said", "Needless to say", "Simply put", "In essence", "At its core", "In the world of", "When it comes to", "At a high level", "As you can see", "As mentioned above", "As noted above", "As previously noted", "As we have seen", "As discussed above", "In this section", "Put simply", "Generally speaking", "Broadly speaking", "The key takeaway", "The fact of the matter is", "It should be noted", "It must be noted", "By way of background".

Never close a section on: "In summary", "In conclusion", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "In short", "All in all", "Overall", "Ultimately", "In closing", "To conclude", "To wrap up", "The takeaway", "Net net", "In a nutshell", "Long story short", "To put it simply", "On the whole".

At most one hedge per claim: "might", "may", "could", "perhaps", "maybe", "possibly", "potentially", "probably", "seems", "appears", "arguably", "somewhat", "relatively", "presumably", "likely", "generally", "typically", "I think", "I believe", "tends to", "to some extent", "in some cases", "apparently", "conceivably", "ostensibly", "seemingly", "in theory", "I suspect", "My sense is".

A cross-reference that names its target stays legitimate, so "As noted above" is banned while "the payout window defined under The weekly cycle" is not. A heading followed by a sentence that shares its words and adds no new one is a heading echo: cut the sentence and open on substance.

### 3.4 The two cut rules the validator settles alone

Both resolve without judgement, so the validator blocks on them in a deliverable and reports them as advice on an instruction file.

**Importance assertion.** A sentence of twelve words or fewer carrying one of "important", "critical", "essential", "crucial", "vital", "matters", "significant", "noteworthy" or "fundamental", and carrying no content word of its own beyond that marker and generic filler. A sentence that names what matters and why is left alone.

**Effort reporting.** A sentence opening on "I" or "We" that reaches one of "analysed", "analyzed", "reviewed", "checked", "scored", "scanned", "verified", "examined", "evaluated", "assessed", "investigated" or "audited" within the next few words. A quoted mention is left alone, and so is a sentence whose subject is the process the artifact documents rather than the author. State what the work found, since the work itself is not the deliverable.

---

## 4. KEEP RULES

The anti-robotic half, at the same weight as the cut list. Each item names what a compression pass destroys first.

- **Semantic connectives.** `because`, `so`, `which means`, `unless`, `otherwise`, `since` carry the logic, and deleting one turns an argument into a pile of assertions. The Human Voice cap on `however`, `furthermore`, `moreover`, `additionally` and `consequently` limits rhetoric and never reaches these
- **One concrete instance per non-obvious rule.** The example is what makes a rule applicable
- **The caveat that prevents a wrong action.** A reader who follows the trimmed version and breaks something was not served by the trim
- **The scope qualifier.** `when`, `only when`, `for X but not Y`. A rule stripped of its scope is applied everywhere
- **The noun behind a pronoun.** Name it again once the referent sits more than a clause away
- **The negative case.** "A path string is not verification" is where the reader learns the boundary
- **The specific number.** 33 fixtures, not several fixtures
- **One human beat per roughly 400 words.** An aside, a judgement, a plain admission of what is unknown
- **Grammar.** Articles, copulas and finite verbs are never a compression target, because conciseness removes claims and never syntax

---

## 5. OVER-COMPRESSION SIGNATURES

### 5.1 The five shapes

- **Connective stripping.** Clauses sit next to each other with the relation deleted, so the reader guesses whether the second causes, qualifies or contradicts the first
- **Referent stripping.** Pronouns and bare nouns left with their antecedents cut away
- **Telegraphese.** Dropped articles and copulas, verbless fragments, headline grammar in body text
- **Condition collapse.** A conditional rule flattened into an absolute one, which is a correctness bug rather than a style one
- **Example deletion.** An abstract rule left with nothing showing what it looks like in use

### 5.2 The two the validator counts, and the perimeter they are measured over

Connective stripping and telegraphese leave a numeric trace, so the validator counts them and blocks on a deliverable below either floor. Repair a document that trips one by naming the deleted relations back in and restoring the subject behind every stranded pronoun, never by adding words.

- **Connective floor.** At least 5 semantic connectives per 1000 words of prose
- **Article floor.** At least 30 articles per 1000 words of prose

Both floors are measured over paragraph prose alone, because a ratio only means something where sentences carry the reasoning. Outside the perimeter: frontmatter, a heading at any level, a bullet, a numbered item, a table row, a blockquote, an image, a horizontal rule, a field line such as `**Placement:** Creator deals dashboard`, a hashtag or handle run, a label line whose whole content is one bold or underlined run such as `**Most authentic**`, anything inside a fenced code block, and any HTML comment. Below 200 words of paragraph prose neither floor is applied, since a ratio over fewer words than that is noise.

---

## 7. FORMAT

Prose, bullets and tables are not interchangeable, and picking wrong is how a short answer still reads badly. Three questions decide and the first yes wins: prose where the items differ in weight or their order encodes reasoning, a table where every row shares the same fields, bullets where the items are parallel, independently actionable and three to seven in number. Anything reaching the end without a yes is one paragraph pretending to be a list. Over-bulleting is the main way output turns robotic while looking concise, and the tells are verbless fragments, a bullet that needs the one above it to parse, and a list whose connectives were deleted so the items would line up. Heading density scales with length: under 300 words no headings, above that one per 150 to 400 words.

---

## 8. WHAT A DELIVERABLE NEVER CONTAINS

The reasoning that produced an artifact, the score it earned and the assumptions it rests on are real work, and they belong in the reply beside the export path rather than inside the file the reader opens.

### 8.1 The enumeration

- A scoring section of any kind, whether headed MEQT, HVR, DEAL scoring, Scoring, Self-scan, Hard blockers or Weakest
- A dimension breakdown line, such as `M 4 · E 6 · Q 6 · T 3 · D 3` or its `D · E · A · L` equivalent
- A total, a floor status, a pass or fail verdict, or a score band action
- A hard blocker count or a voice self-scan line, in any wording
- Score commentary, such as a line opening `Weakest:` and naming which dimensions were thin
- An improvement-cycle note, an iteration count or a re-score history
- A bracketed `[Assumes: ...]` tag
- A methodology transcript, a perspective roster, an energy level or a phase-flow trace
- A validation checklist, a gate roster or a template-compliance report
- An attestation footer, a Mode header in visible text, a Template version in visible text, or any other processing metadata

### 8.2 The one sanctioned exception

Line 1 may carry a single HTML comment header, which renders as nothing and is the designed home for the mode, the framework, the score and the template version. A `Stats:` or `Assumes:` line written as an HTML comment directly below sits inside the same exception, for the same reason. Invisible when rendered is the whole test, so a score written as visible text is a violation wherever it sits in the file and a score written as a comment is fine wherever it sits.

### 8.3 Where the reporting goes instead

The reply carries what the artifact does not: the export path with read-back confirmation where the runtime can write files, the score and its verdict at the depth the mode calls for, the voice self-scan line naming the terms fixed and the terms kept with their reason, the assumptions in a form the user can correct before they harden, a short summary and one next step. Producing that report is the point, and moving it out of the artifact does not make it optional.

### 8.4 Two narrow overrides

Where the artifact refines a supplied source, never inject a Mode, Template, Perspectives, Quality Score or Energy header into preserved source structure, since the comment header is for a new artifact and a refinement keeps the source's own opening. Where the packaging renders the deliverable in a panel instead of saving a file, that rendered block is the artifact and the enumeration applies to it unchanged, the report follows the block, and the path is reported as export-equivalent rather than claimed as a save.

---

## 12. THE PRE-EXPORT PASS

Run this after the voice pass and before the export, in order. The first two steps are the cut side and the last three are the keep side, and running only the cut side is the failure this layer exists to prevent.

1. Delete every opener, recap and hedge stack named in Section 3.2, both shapes named in Section 3.4, and the question echo, intent narration, compliance acknowledgement and closing recap the body already carries, including the sentences after the phrase that opened one
2. Apply the reconstruction test to every remaining cut you are tempted to make, and stop at the first one that fails
3. Name every relation a reader would otherwise guess, then repair referent stripping, telegraphese and condition collapse in place
4. Confirm one concrete instance survives per non-obvious rule, one caveat survives per action that could go wrong, and the format matches the content under Section 7
5. Confirm the body carries nothing from Section 8.1, and that everything removed at this step now sits in the reply. This step is skipped most often, because the process material was correct work and deleting correct work feels wrong. It is not deleted, it moves

17	Task-mode guidance aligned to the current Product Owner task corpus. This version prioritizes a flexible context block, numbered requirement groups, an H2 About and H3 section headings under it.

28	
29	## 1. OVERVIEW
30	
31	### Purpose
32	
33	Provides the task-mode workflow, delivery standards and structure rules for `$task` and `$t` requests. Task Mode creates or refines Product Owner tasks that define WHAT and WHY, delivered as a markdown task artifact with checklist items inside Requirements for QA and handoff.
34	
35	### When to Use
36	
37	Use Task Mode for:
38	- Standalone tasks with About and Requirements
39	- Synced tasks updated to match pasted source material or corpus style
40	- Parent tasks that link or track child subtasks
41	- Subtasks covering one area within a parent task
42	- Feature work, enhancements, acceptance criteria and refinement of existing task content
43	
44	### Command: `$task`
45	
46	- **Short Alias:** `$t`
47	- **Purpose:** Create or refine Product Owner tasks that define WHAT and WHY
48	- **Output:** Markdown task artifact
49	- **Thinking:** Rigor scales with the selected energy automatically
50	- **Interactive Mode:** Ask one comprehensive question unless the request already contains enough direction. An explicit command routes the request and does not stand in for the direction, so `$task` and `$bug` still ask their context-specific question and wait. Only `$quick` may skip routine intake
51	- **Key Feature:** Uses checklist items inside Requirements for QA and handoff
52	
53	### Core Rules
54	
55	- Ask one comprehensive question before drafting unless the request already contains enough direction or uses `$quick`. An explicit command routes the request and does not supply that direction
56	- Enough direction never covers a scope the model would have to choose: when a supplied source splits the work across teams, owners, surfaces or tickets and the request names none of them, the scope is missing, so the first reply is the one question with no draft
57	- Deliver only the requested task, subtask or refinement
58	- Do not force a fixed metadata block order when the source task already exists
59	- When syncing or refining an existing task, preserve the source section names, section order and reference labels unless the user asks to standardize them. A value, name or status a supplied source gives travels into the task as the source writes it, inside backticks: a value a requirement builds or checks, such as an algorithm, header, endpoint, status code, count, range, timeout, schedule or threshold, an event, property or service name, and a status word such as `deprecated` or `proposed`. A supplied value is a constraint rather than HOW, so staying in WHAT and WHY never removes it. Say what a status means beside its word, never in place of it, and never write a generic stand-in such as the server where the source names the service
60	- Use the same filename when updating an existing task
61	
62	### Task Types Supported
63	
64	- **Standalone task:** Full task with About and Requirements
65	- **Synced task:** Existing task updated to match pasted source material or corpus style
66	- **Parent task:** Coordination task that links or tracks child subtasks
67	- **Subtask:** Narrow task covering one area within a parent task
68	
69	---
70	
71	## 2. DELIVERY STANDARDS
72	
73	### Required Core Sections
74	
75	Every task must include:
76	
77	1. Title
78	2. `## About`
79	3. `### Requirements`
80	
81	### Optional Context Sections
82	
83	Use only when they add value or already exist in the source task:
84	
85	- `**References**`
86	- `**Epic**`
87	- `**Parent task**`
88	- `**Related tasks**`
89	- `**Related tickets**`
90	- `**Ticket:** TBD`
91	- `Flows`
92	- `Page`
93	- `Components` or `Component`
94	- `**User Story**`
95	
96	### Flexibility Rules
97	
98	- The task corpus contains both newer clean tasks and older legacy tasks
99	- The template must support either a minimal context block or a richer context block
100	- Category headings inside Requirements are optional but recommended for larger tasks
101	- Category headings may be bold or plain when matching existing source material
102	
103	### Requirement Item Standard
104	
105	Each numbered requirement group should follow this pattern unless the source task must be mirrored more literally:
106	
107	1. Numbered item title
108	2. One or more short paragraphs that explain the outcome and context
109	3. `**Checklist**`
110	4. `- []` checklist items for literal, actionable requirements
111	5. Checklist and bullet items must not end with `.`
112	
113	Number requirement groups only when the task carries two or more. A single group keeps its bold title without a number. The moment a second group appears, number them `1.`, `2.` in order.
114	
115	### Assumptions
116	
117	- Never add `[Assumes: ...]` in task exports
118	- If dependency uncertainty matters, rewrite it as plain task language without bracketed assumption tags
119	- A short blockquoted note after a requirement block is acceptable when it clarifies terminology, behavior distinctions or intentionally deferred logic that affects QA
120	
121	---
122	
123	## 3. STRUCTURE RULES
124	
125	### Section Hierarchy
126	
127	- **Core sections:** `## About` at H2, `### Requirements` at H3
128	- **Requirement category headings:** `### **{Group Name}**` or `### {Group Name}` when matching an existing task
129	- **Bold sub-label:** `**Checklist**`
130	- **Optional bold labels:** `**References**`, `**Epic**`, `**Parent task**`, `**Related tickets**`
131	
132	### Naming a parent or related work with no link
133	
134	A parent task, related task, ticket or epic is often named before it exists as a link. Give it its own bullet as backticked plain text, `` - `{Task title}` ``, which is the shape `**Epic**` already uses. Never fabricate a ClickUp or Figma URL to complete the link, never drop the named parent because no link was supplied, and never push it into About as prose where a reader looking for the relationship will not find it. When the link arrives later, the bullet becomes an ordinary markdown link in place. Paired FigJam outputs follow the handoff, read-back and link-placement contract in Flow Mode Section 8.
135	
136	### Divider Rules
137	
138	- Use `---` after `## About`
139	- Use `---` after `### Requirements`
140	- Use `---` after each category heading
141	- Use `---` after each numbered item title
142	
143	### References Block
144	
145	The references block is flexible. Use only the subsections that matter.
146	
147	Allowed reference labels include:
148	
149	- `Flows`
150	- `Page`
151	- `Components`
152	- `Component`
153	- `Changed`
154	- `Impacted`
155	
156	These labels may be bold or plain when syncing an existing task. Do not auto-normalize them unless the user asks.
157	
158	### Requirement Group Variants
159	
160	The active template supports three valid patterns:
161	
162	#### Pattern A: Flat numbered groups
163	
164	Use when the task is small.
165	
166	```markdown
167	1.  **{Item Title}**
168	
169	---
170	
171	{Short description.}
172	
173	**Checklist**
174	
175	- [] {Requirement}
176	- [] {Requirement}
177	```
178	
179	#### Pattern B: Category heading plus numbered groups
180	
181	Use when the task spans multiple areas.
182	
183	```markdown
184	### **{Category Name}**
185	
186	---
187	
188	1.  **{Item Title}**
189	
190	---
191	
192	{Short description.}
193	
194	**Checklist**
195	
196	- [] {Requirement}
197	- [] {Requirement}
198	```
199	
200	#### Pattern C: Nested sub-blocks inside a numbered group
201	
202	Use when one numbered requirement needs several sub-areas.
203	
204	```markdown
205	1.  **{Item Title}**
206	
207	---
208	
209	{Short description.}
210	
211	**Sub-area A**
212	
213	- [] {Requirement}
214	- [] {Requirement}
215	
216	**Sub-area B**
217	
218	- [] {Requirement}
219	```
220	
221	### User Story Usage
222	
223	- User Story is optional
224	- Include it only when it clarifies the user flow or business value
225	- Place it inside the relevant numbered requirement block
226	- Use Given / When / Then format
227	- Use this exact structure only
228	
229	```markdown
230	**User Story**
231	
232	- **Given:** {context}
233	- **When:** {action}
234	- **Then:** {outcome}
235	```
236	
237	The labels carry a colon and the block takes no `---` divider under `**User Story**`, which is what the task corpus writes and what [task-templates.md](../assets/task-templates.md) shows. The divider rules above cover `## About`, `### Requirements`, category headings and numbered item titles, and the bold sub-labels inside a requirement (`**Checklist**`, `**User Story**`) are not among them. A refinement keeps whatever the source task already uses.
238	
239	### Tables
240	
241	Use a table when every row shares the same fields, such as token or property values that change per size.
242	
243	- A table carries at most 4 columns. When the columns would pass that, split them across more tables that each repeat the first column
244	- A table of values that vary by size puts Size in the leftmost column with one row per size. Each token or property gets its own column, though tokens that share every value may share one
245	
246	[`examples/task/task-example-ds-variables.md`](../assets/examples/task/task-example-ds-variables.md) shows both rules on a design token release.
247

249	
250	## 4. QUALITY CHECKLIST
251	
252	### Pre-Creation Validation
253	
254	- [ ] User request understood clearly?
255	- [ ] Task type identified correctly?
256	- [ ] Scope limited to the requested change?
257	- [ ] Source material preserved when task is a sync or refinement?
258	- [ ] Latest template version used?
259	- [ ] Supplied links in References, Epic, Related tasks and Related tickets resolve, with unresolvable ones flagged in prose rather than kept as dead links?
260	
261	### Structure Validation
262	
263	- [ ] Title present as H1?
264	- [ ] About uses `## About`?
265	- [ ] Requirements uses `### Requirements`?
266	- [ ] Numbered requirement groups use clear titles?
267	- [ ] Actionable requirement items use `- []`, with no space between the brackets?
268	- [ ] `---` dividers used consistently?
269	- [ ] Every table at most 4 columns, with Size leftmost when values vary by size?
270	
271	### Content Validation
272	
273	- [ ] About explains the task outcome and value?
274	- [ ] Requirements describe WHAT and WHY, not HOW, and carry every supplied value, name and status word as the source writes it?
275	- [ ] Requirement wording is concrete and testable?
276	- [ ] No unrequested scope added?
277	- [ ] Optional sections included only when useful?
278	- [ ] User Story included only when it adds value?
279	
280	### Source Sync Validation
281	
282	- [ ] Existing headings preserved when user asked for a sync?
283	- [ ] Existing section order preserved when user asked for a sync?
284	- [ ] Existing reference labels preserved when user asked for a sync?
285	- [ ] Legacy `[ ]` boxes or plain bullets converted to `- []` checklists only when the user asked to normalize them?
286	
287	---
288	
289	## 5. ERROR RECOVERY
290	
291	### Common Errors
292	
293	#### Forced metadata block
294	
295	**Fix:** Remove unneeded `Epic`, `Related tickets` or `Ticket` sections. Keep only what the task needs.
296	
297	#### Plain bullets used for actionable requirements
298	
299	**Fix:** Convert requirement bullets to `- []` checklists.
300	
301	#### Source task was standardized when it should have been synced
302	
303	**Fix:** Restore the source section names, order and wording, then update only the checklist or requested parts.
304	
305	#### User Story added by default
306	
307	**Fix:** Remove it unless it adds clear value or the user requested it.
308	
309	#### Assumption tags appear in export
310	
311	**Fix:** Remove `[Assumes: ...]` and rewrite the point in plain task language or remove it if it is not required.
312	
313	### Prevention Rules
314	
315	1. Start from the source task when one exists
316	2. Keep the core sections fixed and the context block flexible
317	3. Group the checklist at the level that best supports verification
318	4. Use `- []` for actionable items
319	5. Add only the sections the task actually needs
320	
321	---
322	
323	Templates: see [task-templates.md](../assets/task-templates.md).
324	
325	---
326	
327	## 6. FINAL REMINDERS
328	
329	- ClickUp delivery offers and approval follow `SKILL.md` Section 7, ClickUp Handoff
330	
331	1. Keep the core structure fixed and the context block flexible
332	2. Preserve source structure when syncing an existing task
333	3. Use category headings when they make the task easier to scan
334	4. Use `- []` for actionable requirement items
335	5. Stay in WHAT and WHY, not HOW
336	6. Deliver only the requested task scope
337	---
338	
339	When To Use list:
340	
341	- Development tasks, subtasks, parent tasks, acceptance criteria, QA-ready requirements, and copy-consistency or casing standardisation work
342	- Bug reports, defect writeups, reproduction steps, expected behavior, capture
343	- Refinement of pasted task, bug, Story or document content into backlog-ready or ClickUp-ready markdown
344	- Stories and Epics with Connextra-adjacent house-format sections, numbered Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and a Mark-as-done checkbox per criterion
345	- Product or engineering guides, catalogs, behavior references, runbooks, API or schema references, architecture documents, technical proposals and decision records
346	
347	Backlog artefact rule:
348	
349	5. Keep backlog artifacts outcome-focused. Keep documentation facts, analysis, recommendations and proposals in their correct authority state.
350	
351	Dependency and edge case rule:
352	
353	9. Identify dependencies, edge cases, error states, empty states, loading states and permission boundaries when relevant.
354	
355	Acceptance criteria rule:
356

# Product Owner - Templates - Task Mode

Task-mode guidance aligned to the current Product Owner task corpus. This version prioritizes a flexible context block, numbered requirement groups, an H2 About and H3 section headings under it.

**Loading Condition:** ON-DEMAND
**Purpose:** Provides task-mode workflow, standards and structure rules for `$task` and `$t` requests
**Scope:** Task mode overview, delivery standards, structure rules, error recovery and task template usage pointer
**Output Path:** `export/[existing-task-name].md` or `export/[###] - task-[description].md`. Story bundle task paths and the `$story $task` conflict follow the contract in `story-mode.md` Section 7.
**Loads With:** `assets/task-templates.md` as the paired scaffold, beside the always-loaded `references/hvr-core.md` and `references/conciseness.md`
**Routed By:** `$task`, `$t`, `$task --subtask`, task framing, the feature, acceptance, user_need, technical_task and integration semantic topics, and the ui_refinement topic on its 0.80 override
**Hands Off To:** `references/interactive-mode.md` when scope, user value or testable acceptance criteria cannot be inferred, which returns here once the user answers

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Provides the task-mode workflow, delivery standards and structure rules for `$task` and `$t` requests. Task Mode creates or refines Product Owner tasks that define WHAT and WHY, delivered as a markdown task artifact with checklist items inside Requirements for QA and handoff.

### When to Use

Use Task Mode for:
- Standalone tasks with About and Requirements
- Synced tasks updated to match pasted source material or corpus style
- Parent tasks that link or track child subtasks
- Subtasks covering one area within a parent task
- Feature work, enhancements, acceptance criteria and refinement of existing task content

### Command: `$task`

- **Short Alias:** `$t`
- **Purpose:** Create or refine Product Owner tasks that define WHAT and WHY
- **Output:** Markdown task artifact
- **Thinking:** Rigor scales with the selected energy automatically
- **Interactive Mode:** Ask one comprehensive question unless the request already contains enough direction. An explicit command routes the request and does not stand in for the direction, so `$task` and `$bug` still ask their context-specific question and wait. Only `$quick` may skip routine intake
- **Key Feature:** Uses checklist items inside Requirements for QA and handoff

### Core Rules

- Ask one comprehensive question before drafting unless the request already contains enough direction or uses `$quick`. An explicit command routes the request and does not supply that direction
- Enough direction never covers a scope the model would have to choose: when a supplied source splits the work across teams, owners, surfaces or tickets and the request names none of them, the scope is missing, so the first reply is the one question with no draft
- Deliver only the requested task, subtask or refinement
- Do not force a fixed metadata block order when the source task already exists
- When syncing or refining an existing task, preserve the source section names, section order and reference labels unless the user asks to standardize them. A value, name or status a supplied source gives travels into the task as the source writes it, inside backticks: a value a requirement builds or checks, such as an algorithm, header, endpoint, status code, count, range, timeout, schedule or threshold, an event, property or service name, and a status word such as `deprecated` or `proposed`. A supplied value is a constraint rather than HOW, so staying in WHAT and WHY never removes it. Say what a status means beside its word, never in place of it, and never write a generic stand-in such as the server where the source names the service
- Use the same filename when updating an existing task

### Task Types Supported

- **Standalone task:** Full task with About and Requirements
- **Synced task:** Existing task updated to match pasted source material or corpus style
- **Parent task:** Coordination task that links or tracks child subtasks
- **Subtask:** Narrow task covering one area within a parent task

---

## 2. DELIVERY STANDARDS

### Required Core Sections

Every task must include:

1. Title
2. `## About`
3. `### Requirements`

### Optional Context Sections

Use only when they add value or already exist in the source task:

- `**References**`
- `**Epic**`
- `**Parent task**`
- `**Related tasks**`
- `**Related tickets**`
- `**Ticket:** TBD`
- `Flows`
- `Page`
- `Components` or `Component`
- `**User Story**`

### Flexibility Rules

- The task corpus contains both newer clean tasks and older legacy tasks
- The template must support either a minimal context block or a richer context block
- Category headings inside Requirements are optional but recommended for larger tasks
- Category headings may be bold or plain when matching existing source material

### Requirement Item Standard

Each numbered requirement group should follow this pattern unless the source task must be mirrored more literally:

1. Numbered item title
2. One or more short paragraphs that explain the outcome and context
3. `**Checklist**`
4. `- []` checklist items for literal, actionable requirements
5. Checklist and bullet items must not end with `.`

Number requirement groups only when the task carries two or more. A single group keeps its bold title without a number. The moment a second group appears, number them `1.`, `2.` in order.

### Assumptions

- Never add `[Assumes: ...]` in task exports
- If dependency uncertainty matters, rewrite it as plain task language without bracketed assumption tags
- A short blockquoted note after a requirement block is acceptable when it clarifies terminology, behavior distinctions or intentionally deferred logic that affects QA

---

## 3. STRUCTURE RULES

### Section Hierarchy

- **Core sections:** `## About` at H2, `### Requirements` at H3
- **Requirement category headings:** `### **{Group Name}**` or `### {Group Name}` when matching an existing task
- **Bold sub-label:** `**Checklist**`
- **Optional bold labels:** `**References**`, `**Epic**`, `**Parent task**`, `**Related tickets**`

### Naming a parent or related work with no link

A parent task, related task, ticket or epic is often named before it exists as a link. Give it its own bullet as backticked plain text, `` - `{Task title}` ``, which is the shape `**Epic**` already uses. Never fabricate a ClickUp or Figma URL to complete the link, never drop the named parent because no link was supplied, and never push it into About as prose where a reader looking for the relationship will not find it. When the link arrives later, the bullet becomes an ordinary markdown link in place. Paired FigJam outputs follow the handoff, read-back and link-placement contract in Flow Mode Section 8.

### Divider Rules

- Use `---` after `## About`
- Use `---` after `### Requirements`
- Use `---` after each category heading
- Use `---` after each numbered item title

### References Block

The references block is flexible. Use only the subsections that matter.

Allowed reference labels include:

- `Flows`
- `Page`
- `Components`
- `Component`
- `Changed`
- `Impacted`

These labels may be bold or plain when syncing an existing task. Do not auto-normalize them unless the user asks.

### Requirement Group Variants

The active template supports three valid patterns:

#### Pattern A: Flat numbered groups

Use when the task is small.

```markdown
1.  **{Item Title}**

---

{Short description.}

**Checklist**

- [] {Requirement}
- [] {Requirement}
```

#### Pattern B: Category heading plus numbered groups

Use when the task spans multiple areas.

```markdown
### **{Category Name}**

---

1.  **{Item Title}**

---

{Short description.}

**Checklist**

- [] {Requirement}
- [] {Requirement}
```

#### Pattern C: Nested sub-blocks inside a numbered group

Use when one numbered requirement needs several sub-areas.

```markdown
1.  **{Item Title}**

---

{Short description.}

**Sub-area A**

- [] {Requirement}
- [] {Requirement}

**Sub-area B**

- [] {Requirement}
```

### User Story Usage

- User Story is optional
- Include it only when it clarifies the user flow or business value
- Place it inside the relevant numbered requirement block
- Use Given / When / Then format
- Use this exact structure only

```markdown
**User Story**

- **Given:** {context}
- **When:** {action}
- **Then:** {outcome}
```

The labels carry a colon and the block takes no `---` divider under `**User Story**`, which is what the task corpus writes and what [task-templates.md](../assets/task-templates.md) shows. The divider rules above cover `## About`, `### Requirements`, category headings and numbered item titles, and the bold sub-labels inside a requirement (`**Checklist**`, `**User Story**`) are not among them. A refinement keeps whatever the source task already uses.

### Tables

Use a table when every row shares the same fields, such as token or property values that change per size.

- A table carries at most 4 columns. When the columns would pass that, split them across more tables that each repeat the first column
- A table of values that vary by size puts Size in the leftmost column with one row per size. Each token or property gets its own column, though tokens that share every value may share one

[`examples/task/task-example-ds-variables.md`](../assets/examples/task/task-example-ds-variables.md) shows both rules on a design token release.

---

## 4. QUALITY CHECKLIST

### Pre-Creation Validation

- [ ] User request understood clearly?
- [ ] Task type identified correctly?
- [ ] Scope limited to the requested change?
- [ ] Source material preserved when task is a sync or refinement?
- [ ] Latest template version used?
- [ ] Supplied links in References, Epic, Related tasks and Related tickets resolve, with unresolvable ones flagged in prose rather than kept as dead links?

### Structure Validation

- [ ] Title present as H1?
- [ ] About uses `## About`?
- [ ] Requirements uses `### Requirements`?
- [ ] Numbered requirement groups use clear titles?
- [ ] Actionable requirement items use `- []`, with no space between the brackets?
- [ ] `---` dividers used consistently?
- [ ] Every table at most 4 columns, with Size leftmost when values vary by size?

### Content Validation

- [ ] About explains the task outcome and value?
- [ ] Requirements describe WHAT and WHY, not HOW, and carry every supplied value, name and status word as the source writes it?
- [ ] Requirement wording is concrete and testable?
- [ ] No unrequested scope added?
- [ ] Optional sections included only when useful?
- [ ] User Story included only when it adds value?

### Source Sync Validation

- [ ] Existing headings preserved when user asked for a sync?
- [ ] Existing section order preserved when user asked for a sync?
- [ ] Existing reference labels preserved when user asked for a sync?
- [ ] Legacy `[ ]` boxes or plain bullets converted to `- []` checklists only when the user asked to normalize them?

---

## 5. ERROR RECOVERY

### Common Errors

#### Forced metadata block

**Fix:** Remove unneeded `Epic`, `Related tickets` or `Ticket` sections. Keep only what the task needs.

#### Plain bullets used for actionable requirements

**Fix:** Convert requirement bullets to `- []` checklists.

#### Source task was standardized when it should have been synced

**Fix:** Restore the source section names, order and wording, then update only the checklist or requested parts.

#### User Story added by default

**Fix:** Remove it unless it adds clear value or the user requested it.

#### Assumption tags appear in export

**Fix:** Remove `[Assumes: ...]` and rewrite the point in plain task language or remove it if it is not required.

### Prevention Rules

1. Start from the source task when one exists
2. Keep the core sections fixed and the context block flexible
3. Group the checklist at the level that best supports verification
4. Use `- []` for actionable items
5. Add only the sections the task actually needs

---

Templates: see [task-templates.md](../assets/task-templates.md).

---

## 6. FINAL REMINDERS

- ClickUp delivery offers and approval follow `SKILL.md` Section 7, ClickUp Handoff

1. Keep the core structure fixed and the context block flexible
2. Preserve source structure when syncing an existing task
3. Use category headings when they make the task easier to scan
4. Use `- []` for actionable requirement items
5. Stay in WHAT and WHY, not HOW
6. Deliver only the requested task scope
---

When To Use list:

- Development tasks, subtasks, parent tasks, acceptance criteria, QA-ready requirements, and copy-consistency or casing standardisation work
- Bug reports, defect writeups, reproduction steps, expected behavior, capture
- Refinement of pasted task, bug, Story or document content into backlog-ready or ClickUp-ready markdown
- Stories and Epics with Connextra-adjacent house-format sections, numbered Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and a Mark-as-done checkbox per criterion
- Product or engineering guides, catalogs, behavior references, runbooks, API or schema references, architecture documents, technical proposals and decision records

Backlog artefact rule:

5. Keep backlog artifacts outcome-focused. Keep documentation facts, analysis, recommendations and proposals in their correct authority state.

Dependency and edge case rule:

9. Identify dependencies, edge cases, error states, empty states, loading states and permission boundaries when relevant.

Acceptance criteria rule:

10. Write acceptance criteria as outcomes the user can rely on, few in number and open on the mechanism, growing only with the surfaces a story touches. In a Story, Requirements holds hard constraints only, carries every hard value the source supplied with its value, units and notation intact, mirrors the source's own screen or surface grouping where it has one, names each shared screen's reuse map as a constraint, and is omitted only where the source supplies none. Every Requirements item is a `- []` checkbox holding a sentence a build can fail, so an item that reports what a screen says, shows or contains, naming no value, limit, condition, effect or named flow a build could get wrong, is description and is struck rather than reworded, and copy a screenshot supplies is quoted verbatim in backticks or dropped. A supplied value never travels into an acceptance criterion instead. Keep the Task QA checklist inside a Task's Requirements.

20	
21	Copy/apply response templates for Product Owner interactive intake, and the one reply shape every delivery and clarification reply follows.
22	
23	**Loading Condition:** Section 3 ALWAYS, before the first reply of a session. Sections 1 and 2 CONDITIONAL, with `references/interactive-mode.md` whenever a request reaches the one-question flow
24	**Purpose:** Provides the intake prompts each artifact lane asks when required information is missing, so one question covers every unresolved decision, and the delivery reply shape every other surface points at
25	**Scope:** The comprehensive question, the Task, Bug, Story and Doc context questions, the source-authority question, the response formatting rules and the delivery reply shape with its worked replies
26	**Output Path:** `export/[###] - {task|bug|doc|Story|Epic}-[description]-clarification.md`
27	
28	---
29	
30	## 1. OVERVIEW
31	
32	### Purpose
33	
34	Provides reusable multi-line markdown prompts for default intake, task-specific intake, bug-specific intake, Story intake and product- or engineering-document creation or refinement.
35	
36	### Usage
37	
38	Load this asset with Interactive Mode. Copy the appropriate question template, keep the multi-line markdown structure and ask one consolidated question before waiting for the user. For Doc requests, populate only unresolved fields and list every known source conflict in the same question. When artifact commands conflict, include artifact selection and any conditional Doc fields together so one response can resolve routing and Doc context. Do not end a newly authored or rewritten bullet item with a full stop.
39	
40	---
41	
42	## 2. RESPONSE TEMPLATES
43	
44	**CRITICAL: All templates must be multi-line markdown. Never convert to single-line text.**
45	
46	### Comprehensive Question (Default)
47	
48	```markdown
49	Welcome! Let's create exactly what you need.
50	
51	Please provide the following information at once:
52	
53	[If artifact commands conflict: I detected these deliverables: {detected_artifacts}. Choose one primary deliverable and complete its relevant fields below.]
54	
55	**0. How should I work this?**
56	- Quick - lean pass with smart defaults, minimal back-and-forth
57	- Deeper - take more time, read more context and apply the full phase flow
58	
59	**1. Deliverable type:**
60	- Task - Development task with QA checklist
61	- Bug - Defect report with evidence and reproduction steps
62	- Story - A Story or Epic in the Barter house format, new or refined, with numbered Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, and Connextra lines or Definition of Ready/Done gates only where the artifact earns them
63	- Doc - Product or engineering guide, catalog, behavior reference, runbook, technical reference, or proposal; new or refined
64	
65	**If the deliverable is a board:**
66	- Who reads it, which question it answers and what that reader should decide after reading it
67	- Leave it blank and I read all three from the sources and mark them assumed
68	
69	**2. Scope & complexity:**
70	- For tasks: Backend/Frontend/Mobile/Full-stack/DevOps/QA
71	- For bugs: Platform, affected area, severity and reproduction context
72	- For Stories: Create or refine, the user role and value, how many requirements, and whether they share one mechanism
73	- For docs: Create or refine, product/engineering/mixed domain, purpose, audience, required technical depth, requested scope and preferred shape if known
74	
75	**3. Requirements:**
76	- What needs to be built/fixed
77	- Why does this matter? (problem being solved)
78	- What does success look like?
79	- For docs: What should readers understand, decide or do after reading?
80	
81	**4. Sources, authority & status:**
82	- For docs: Source files or links, which source controls any conflict, and whether claims are current behavior, approved direction, proposal, retired material or unknown
83	- For tasks and bugs: References, evidence, dependencies and relevant constraints
84	
85	**5. Additional context:**
86	- Target audience, product or engineering constraints, dependencies
87	- Figma references? Platforms? (iOS / Android / Web / All)
88	
89	**6. Assumptions to challenge:**
90	- What am I likely to assume incorrectly?
91	- What "impossible" options should I consider?
92	```
93	
94	### Task Format Question
95	
96	```markdown
97	I'll create your task. Quick questions:
98	
99	**Format & scope:** Backend/Frontend/Mobile/Full-stack/DevOps/QA
100	**Requirements:** What needs to be built/fixed? Acceptance criteria? Technical constraints?
101	**Design & platform:** Figma links? Platforms? (iOS / Android / Web / All)
102	**Dependencies:** Related or dependent tickets?
103	**Validation:** What am I likely misunderstanding? What constraints should I question?
104	```
105	
106	### Bug Context Question
107	
108	```markdown
109	I'll create your bug report. Quick questions:
110	
111	**Bug details:** Unexpected behavior? Expected behavior? Steps to reproduce?
112	**Environment:** Where does this occur? Platform(s)? (iOS / Android / Web / All)
113	**Design reference:** Figma references showing expected design?
114	**Evidence:** Screenshots, error logs, console output? When first noticed? Known workaround?
115	**Validation:** What should I NOT assume about root cause? Related bug reports?
116	```
117	
118	### Story Context Question
119	
120	Use this when an explicit Story or Epic command selects Story intent, or when Story intent is selected but role, value, requirement shape or artifact kind (Story or Epic) cannot be inferred safely. Populate only unresolved fields and wait once.
121	
122	```markdown
123	I'll create or refine your Story or Epic. Before drafting, I need the unresolved decisions below in one response:
124	
125	**Operation:** New Story or Epic, or refine an existing one? For a refinement, which file - I will preserve its structure and only add or adjust what you name.
126	**Role & value:** Who is the user, and what benefit should the Story deliver? (This becomes the Connextra "As a ..., I want ..., so that ..." line.)
127	**Requirements:** Which concrete requirements should the Story cover? List them for a Story; if there are none - an initiative split across child stories with a Goal - it is an Epic.
128	**Shared machinery:** Do the requirements run through one common mechanism (a pipeline, rule ladder, state machine or lifecycle)? If so, describe it once.
129	**Evidence & links:** Any governing docs, technical identifiers, thresholds or task links to carry into the spec blocks - exact values, please.
130	**Validation:** What am I likely to assume incorrectly about the user or the promise?
131	```
132	
133	### Doc Context and Clarification Question
134	
135	Use this single pattern for new-document intake, refinement intake, missing source authority, source-status ambiguity and contradictory sources. Include only unresolved items, state known conflicts explicitly, then wait once for the complete response.
136	
137	```markdown
138	I'll create or refine the product or engineering document. Before drafting, I need the unresolved decisions below in one response:
139	
140	**Operation, purpose & audience:** Create or refine? What should the document help its readers understand, decide or do, and who are those readers?
141	**Domain & detail:** Is this product, engineering, operational, security, compliance or mixed documentation? What technical HOW, code, architecture, API, schema, data-model, debugging or evidence detail does the audience need?
142	**Source set:** Which files, links or supplied materials may I use? For a refinement, what is the source filename?
143	**Authority & conflicts:** Which source or claim controls each conflict listed here? [List every known conflict or missing canonical source.]
144	**Document status:** Should the result describe current behavior, approved direction, proposal, retired material or unknown?
145	**Scope & shape:** What must be included or excluded? Choose Guide, Catalog, Behavior reference or Proposal/future state, or ask me to infer the shape from the confirmed purpose.
146	**Layout & refinement boundaries:** New documents use the ClickUp `* * *` divider and `*   ` bullet grammar. For a refinement, what exactly should change? I will preserve existing headings, dividers, bullet markers, order, links, identifiers, tables, code fences, status notices and untouched literal copy outside that scope. State whether structural rewriting or ClickUp normalization is explicitly allowed.
147	**Validation:** Which claims remain unverified, and what should I avoid presenting as fact?
148	```
149	
150	---
151	
152	## 3. DELIVERY REPLY SHAPE
153	
154	Every reply after a saved artifact, a saved clarification or a rendered Deliverable Block uses this one shape. `AGENTS.md`, `SKILL.md`, the mode references and the kernel point here instead of restating it. Models copy a worked reply more closely than they follow a rule, so the worked replies below are part of the contract.
155	
156	### Line Order
157	
158	1. The path line: `Path: ` and the repository-relative export path in backticks. In a Claude Project it reads `Export-equivalent path: ` and comes after the Deliverable Block
159	2. `Verified: read-back succeeded; N lines`, on the skill only
160	3. The `HVR self-scan:` line in its exact shape
161	4. One quality line, `Quality: {verdict} | Kind: {kind} | Energy: {energy}`
162	5. Two or three sentences on what the artifact covers
163	6. The `### Open items` heading, then the numbered items or the one line `None identified`
164	7. One closing line
165	
166	A Story bundle repeats lines 1 and 2 for each file, Story first, then gives one `HVR self-scan:` line for the whole bundle. When an export is still blocked after its retry, the reply prints no path line, opens with `Export blocked:` and the reason, and claims no delivery.
167	
168	### The First Line
169	
170	Nothing comes before the path line: no status line, no sentence announcing the reply, no report of the checks and no divider. After the last check, the next words written are the path.
171	
172	- Wrong first line: `Export complete. The task is saved and read back.`
173	- Right first line: ``Path: `export/009 - task-payout-pause.md` ``
174	
175	### The Quality Line
176	
177	- `{verdict}` reads `every floor met` when all six dimensions clear their floors, names the dimension still short when the three-cycle ceiling was reached, such as `Clarity short after three cycles`, and reads `not scored, clarification only` for a clarification
178	- For a Doc, `{verdict}` names the five Doc checks in order, each `pass` or `attention`, and an attention names its item in brackets: `Source safety pass, Shape fit pass, ClickUp layout attention (two headings missing the trailing divider), Readability pass, Voice pass`
179	- `{kind}` is Task, Subtask, Parent task, Bug, Story, Epic, Story bundle, or Doc with its shape, such as `Doc (Guide)`
180	- `{energy}` is Quick, Standard or Deep
181	
182	The line keeps the pipe separators with a space on each side, carries no bold and holds nothing else. The checks behind it run silently, so no checklist, gate roster, validation display or note about a check that did not run appears anywhere in the reply.
183	
184	### Open Items
185	
186	Every addition, assumption, safe default and unresolved point goes here, never into a second question and never into prose elsewhere in the reply. Number each item from 1 with its topic in bold, such as `1. **Owner time zone**`. Directly below it, indented three spaces, come two bullets: `- **Situation:**` followed on the same line by what the source said or what you added, then `- **Open:**` followed on the same line by what the user should confirm or strike. The text after each label starts with a capital.
187	
188	No blank line sits inside an item or between items, because claude.ai joins a label that stands on a line of its own to the line above it, while a bullet keeps its own line whatever the spacing. An item with nothing left to confirm keeps its number, and its Open bullet reads `Nothing to confirm`. When nothing applies, the section holds the one line `None identified`.
189	
190	### The Closing Line
191	
192	- After a delivered artifact on a `then: "FLOW"` route: the Flow Mode playback, with no ClickUp offer
193	- After a delivered artifact, when ClickUp tooling is available and one list or doc in the push targets file fits: `Want me to push this to {name}, or upload it as a private ClickUp doc instead?`
194	- After a delivered artifact, when ClickUp tooling is available and more than one could fit: `Should this go to {name} or {name}, or should I upload it as a private ClickUp doc instead?`
195	- After a delivered artifact, when ClickUp tooling is available and none fits or the push targets file is absent: `Where in ClickUp should this go? Send a list link, or I'll upload it as a private doc, which I recommend for now.`
196	- After a delivered artifact otherwise: `Want me to change anything?`
197	- After a clarification: `Answer in one message and I'll draft the {kind}.`, naming the kind and never the artifact's path
198	
199	Nothing follows the closing line. On a `then: "FLOW"` route the ClickUp offer comes at the end of the pair instead, once the board link is written back and the artifact is re-saved, because a push before that link would carry no board into ClickUp.
200	
201	### Rules For Every Line
202	
203	- No bullet ends with a full stop, Open items included
204	- No em dash and no semicolon in reply prose
205	- No absolute or temporary path, only the repository-relative export path
206	- The skill reply never pastes the artifact
207	
208	### Worked Replies
209	
210	A delivered task on the skill:
211	
212	```text
213	Path: `export/009 - task-payout-pause.md`
214	Verified: read-back succeeded; 58 lines
215	HVR self-scan: 0 hard blockers. Fixed: none. Kept with reason: none.
216	Quality: every floor met | Kind: Task | Energy: Standard
217	
218	The task pauses creator payouts while a dispute is open and restarts them once Finance closes it. It covers the payout screen banner, the paused state in the admin list and the restart rule.
219	
220	### Open items
221	1. **Restart cut-off**
222	   - **Situation:** The brief names Finance as the owner but gives no time zone for the restart cut-off
223	   - **Open:** Confirm the cut-off runs on Europe/Amsterdam time
224	2. **Empty state**
225	   - **Situation:** I added an empty state for an admin list with no paused payouts
226	   - **Open:** Strike it if the list can never be empty
